note: Billionaire Life prototype. Every date and number below appears in at least one cited source. Situations and outcomes are summarized in our own words and simplified. Alternatives are generic choices for the game, not claims about what he considered.

person.name: Warren Buffett
person.role: Chairman Emeritus and director of Berkshire Hathaway
person.bio: Born in 1930. After a year and a half in New York, where he worked alongside Ben Graham from 1954, he moved back to Omaha in 1956 and built Berkshire Hathaway from there. He handed the CEO job to Greg Abel at the end of 2025 and stopped writing Berkshire's annual letter.

bioSource.title: Warren Buffett's Thanksgiving letter to shareholders

school.name: Value investing, Berkshire style
school.tagline: Buy durable businesses you understand at sensible prices, then own them for a very long time.

principles.name: Durable businesses (economic moats)
principles.summary: He looks for businesses he understands that have a lasting edge, like being the low-cost producer or owning a world-famous brand, which keeps rivals from eating their profits. In his words, "A moat that must be continuously rebuilt will eventually be no moat at all." Charlie Munger pushed him to prefer wonderful businesses at fair prices over fair businesses at wonderful prices.

principles.name: Price is not value
principles.summary: He separates what a stock costs today from what the business is worth, which he defines as the cash it can hand out over its remaining life, discounted to today. He quotes his teacher Ben Graham: "Price is what you pay; value is what you get."

sources.title: An Owner's Manual (updated version of the 1996 booklet)

principles.name: Think like an owner, hold for years
principles.summary: He treats a share as part ownership of a real business, not a ticker to trade, and asks shareholders to see themselves the same way. For outstanding businesses with outstanding managers, he wrote, "our favorite holding period is forever."

sources.title: An Owner's Manual (updated version of the 1996 booklet)

principles.name: Allocate the money, trust able managers
principles.summary: At Berkshire he mainly decided where money went and who ran each business, then left day-to-day decisions to those managers. He described delegating "almost to the point of abdication."

sources.title: An Owner's Manual (updated version of the 1996 booklet)

decisions.title: Take the quick profit or dig in?
decisions.situation: Your investment partnership owns about 7% of Berkshire Hathaway, a struggling New England textile maker you started buying at $7.50 a share in December 1962. The boss agreed to buy you out at $11.50, then the company's formal offer came in at $11.375, an eighth of a point lower.

options.label: Take the $11.375 offer and move on
Refuse, buy more shares and take control
Keep your 7% stake and wait quietly

decisions.actual: Annoyed by the lowball, he did not sell and bought aggressively instead. By April 1965 his partnership owned 392,633 of 1,017,547 shares and took control at a board meeting in early May 1965. He later called refusing the offer a monumentally stupid decision.
decisions.outcome: The textile business kept struggling and he shut it down in 1985. But Berkshire became his vehicle for buying other businesses, starting with insurer National Indemnity for $8.6 million in 1967. From 1965 through 2025, Berkshire's per-share market value grew 19.7% a year on average, versus 10.5% for the S&P 500 with dividends.

lesson.takeaway: A cheap price could not rescue a weak business: the textile operation tied up money for nearly two decades until he shut it down in 1985. That lesson, plus Charlie Munger’s advice, pushed him toward buying wonderful businesses at fair prices instead.
lesson.watchOut: Emotion is expensive: he said he refused the offer because he bristled at being lowballed, and he later called that choice monumentally stupid.

decisions.title: Bet big on the world's best-known drink?
decisions.situation: It is summer 1988. You have admired Coca-Cola since selling Cokes around the neighborhood as a kid in 1936, but never owned a share. Since Roberto Goizueta became CEO in 1981, the company has sharpened its focus and overseas sales are taking off.

options.label: Pass: a famous stock is never a bargain
Buy a big stake and plan to hold it for good
Buy a small starter position and watch

decisions.actual: Berkshire bought 14,172,500 Coca-Cola shares in 1988 at a cost of about $592.5 million, and raised the stake to 23,350,000 shares (cost about $1.02 billion) by the end of 1989. He said his favorite holding period for great businesses is forever.
decisions.outcome: Berkshire still owns it. At the end of 2025 it held 9.3% of Coca-Cola, with a cost basis of $1.299 billion and a market value of $27.964 billion, and it collected $816 million in Coke dividends that year alone.

lesson.takeaway: He bought a business with a world-famous brand that he had admired since childhood and kept it for decades: by 2025 it paid Berkshire $816 million a year in dividends on a cost basis of about $1.3 billion.
lesson.watchOut: Holding forever has a cost too: in his 2004 letter he said he only grumbled about sky-high prices for Berkshire’s "Big Four" holdings, Coca-Cola among them, during the stock-market bubble instead of acting, admitting "I talked when I should have walked."

decisions.title: What happens to your fortune?
decisions.situation: Your 474,998 Berkshire Class A shares are worth about $43 billion and make up more than 98% of your net worth. You have to decide how that money will eventually be used.

options.label: Set up your own foundation and give it all at death
Pledge yearly gifts, most of them to the Gates Foundation
Leave most of it in trust for your heirs

decisions.actual: Announced June 25, 2006 and signed the next day: an irrevocable lifetime pledge earmarking 10 million Berkshire Class B shares for the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, with 5% of the remaining balance given each year, plus smaller pledges to four family foundations. Conditions included that Bill or Melinda Gates stay active in running the foundation and that his gifts add to its own spending.
decisions.outcome: By June 2025 the five foundations had received Berkshire shares worth about $60 billion when given, more than his entire 2006 net worth. His remaining shares were then worth about $145 billion, and he says about 99.5% of his estate will go to philanthropy. The yearly pledges end at his death.

sources.title: Berkshire Hathaway Form 8-K with Schedule 13D/A (Amendment No. 52) describing the pledge
Buffett converts A shares and donates B shares to five foundations

lesson.takeaway: Rather than direct every dollar himself, he backed a foundation whose work he said he greatly admired and set a few clear conditions, much as Berkshire backs proven managers and lets them run things.
lesson.watchOut: Backing others means giving up control: beyond his three conditions, the filing says he placed no limits on how the Gates Foundation used or sold the shares.

sources.title: Berkshire Hathaway Form 8-K with Schedule 13D/A (Amendment No. 52) describing the pledge

decisions.title: Rescue a Wall Street giant in a panic?
decisions.situation: It is September 2008 and the financial crisis is raging. Goldman Sachs became a bank holding company two days ago and needs fresh capital. You have long promised to always keep Berkshire flush with cash.

options.label: Sit tight and protect Berkshire's cash
Put in $5 billion on your own tough terms
Buy Goldman shares cheaply on the open market

decisions.actual: On September 23, 2008 Berkshire agreed to buy $5 billion of Goldman preferred stock paying a 10% dividend, callable at a 10% premium, plus warrants to buy $5 billion of common stock at $115 a share for five years. To pay for this and big deals with Wrigley and GE ($14.5 billion in total), he sold parts of holdings he would rather have kept.
decisions.outcome: Goldman's stock sale the next day was oversubscribed. In March 2011 Goldman said it would buy back Berkshire's preferred shares early. That year Goldman, Swiss Re and GE together paid Berkshire $12.8 billion to redeem securities that had been earning it about $1.2 billion a year before tax.

sources.title: Berkshire Hathaway to invest $5 billion in Goldman Sachs
Berkshire Hathaway invests US$5 billion in Goldman Sachs amid global financial crisis

lesson.takeaway: In a panic, few investors have cash to offer, so the one who does can set tough terms: here a 10% dividend plus warrants. It fits his habit of buying quality when it is marked down.
lesson.watchOut: Buying in turbulent markets can also go wrong: in the same 2008 letter he admitted buying ConocoPhillips near the oil-price peak, a mistake he said cost Berkshire several billion dollars.

decisions.title: When do you hand over the keys?
decisions.situation: You have run Berkshire Hathaway for six decades and are in your mid-90s. Vice Chairman Greg Abel already oversees all the non-insurance businesses. Shareholders are gathered in Omaha for Berkshire's annual meeting.

options.label: Stay CEO for as long as you can
Announce Greg Abel as CEO and stay on as chairman
Break Berkshire up before you step aside

decisions.actual: At the May 3, 2025 meeting he said he would recommend Abel as CEO. The board voted unanimously the next day, effective January 1, 2026, with Buffett staying chairman. In November 2025 he said he would stop writing the annual report and speaking at length at the meeting.
decisions.outcome: Abel became CEO on January 1, 2026 and wrote his first annual letter that February. On September 18, 2026 Buffett was named Chairman Emeritus and stayed on the board; longtime director Howard G. Buffett became chairman.

sources.title: Board appoints Greg Abel CEO effective January 1, 2026
Warren Buffett's Thanksgiving letter to shareholders
Warren E. Buffett becomes Chairman Emeritus; Howard G. Buffett elected Chairman

lesson.takeaway: He treated picking the next leader as part of his job, naming Greg Abel while he could still vouch for him in public and stay on as chairman.
lesson.watchOut: A strong successor does not remove every risk: in November 2025 he wrote that Berkshire's size "takes its toll" and that many companies will do better than it over the next decade or two.

sources.title: Warren Buffett's Thanksgiving letter to shareholders

glossary.definition: A public offer by a company or an outside buyer to purchase a large share of a company's stock from its shareholders, usually at a set price for a limited time.
Buffett's image for a lasting competitive advantage, such as low costs or a powerful brand, that protects a business's profits from competitors the way a moat protects a castle.
Generally what you paid for an investment, including costs such as commissions. It is used to work out your gain or loss when you sell.
A share of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, often on a regular schedule.
A report U.S. public companies file with the SEC to announce major events soon after they happen, between their regular annual and quarterly reports.
A type of share that usually has no voting rights but gets paid dividends before common shareholders, and ranks ahead of them if the company is liquidated.
A contract issued by a company that gives the holder the right, but not the duty, to buy (or in some cases sell) its shares at a set price before a set date.
Buffett's definition: the cash a business can hand out over the rest of its life, discounted back to today. It is always an estimate, so two careful people can reach different figures.

source.title: An Owner's Manual (updated version of the 1996 booklet)

glossary.definition: A yearly report a public company sends shareholders about its business and results, usually opening with a letter from the chief executive.
